title: Pattern A: nucleophiles add to C=O

steps.text: Aldehydes and ketones have only C and H on the carbonyl carbon, and neither can leave. So a nucleophile **adds and stays**. A strong nucleophile (Grignard, hydride, acetylide) attacks directly; acid workup then protonates the O⁻ to an alcohol.
Watch the two arrows: the C–Mg bond attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π bond moves onto oxygen.
Same pattern on an aldehyde. The first arrow is drawn; add the second.
NaBH4 turns cyclohexanone into cyclohexanol. Why is there no new carbon in the product?

options.text: NaBH4 delivers hydride (H⁻), so the new bond to the carbonyl carbon is C–H, not C–C.
options.explains: Right. Same pattern A attack, but the nucleophile is H⁻. Grignards deliver a carbon, which is why they make new C–C bonds.
The oxygen stays; it becomes the alcohol OH after workup. Removing the O entirely (C=O → CH2) needs Wolff–Kishner or Clemmensen.

options.text: Boron bonds to the carbonyl carbon and is removed in workup.
options.explains: Boron ends up on oxygen (as an alkoxyborate), not carbon. The carbonyl carbon gets a hydrogen.

steps.text: Weaker nucleophiles (water, alcohols, amines) need **acid**: protonating the C=O oxygen makes the carbon much more electrophilic. After adding, the O can leave as water, so you get **acetals** (2 ROH), **imines** (1° amine) or **enamines** (2° amine).
Cyclohexanone + pyrrolidine (a 2° amine) with acid gives an enamine, not an imine. Why?

options.text: After water leaves, the nitrogen has no H left to lose, so a proton is removed from the α-carbon instead, giving C=C–N.
options.explains: Right. A 1° amine's N keeps an H that it can lose to form C=N (imine). A 2° amine's N has none, so the α-C–H gives it up.

options.text: Pyrrolidine is too bulky to attack the carbonyl.
options.explains: It attacks just fine (that's the first step). The difference is what happens after water leaves.
2° amines are good nucleophiles. The outcome differs because the N has no N–H left at the end.

steps.text: Last one: draw both arrows yourself.
Which carbonyl compound gives a **2°** alcohol with CH3MgBr, then H3O+?

options.text: An aldehyde other than formaldehyde, such as propanal.
options.explains: Right: the carbonyl carbon already has one carbon group, the Grignard adds a second, so it ends up with two (2°).
Formaldehyde's carbon has no carbon groups, so after the Grignard adds one it's a 1° alcohol.
A ketone's carbon already has two carbon groups; the Grignard adds a third, giving a 3° alcohol.
Esters take two equivalents of Grignard (add, eliminate, add again), giving a 3° alcohol.
